lead: Layering splits a network job into levels, so a change at one level leaves the others alone. Each level talks to its peer at the far end and hands data down through a clear interface. Optics is the bottom level and carries bits for every layer above. Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is a fixed-cell layer-2 design that once promised voice, video and data on one optical pipe. This chapter maps layers, data units and ATM, and shows why IP won.
prereq: You need: 6.5 for nodes, links and lightpaths, and 6.6 for SONET as the carrier underneath.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this at this depth. The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model has seven layers; each layer adds a header or trailer and passes a protocol data unit (PDU) down.

items: Application: user services such as web and e-mail.
Session: start and end a dialogue.
Transport: end-to-end delivery and flow control.
Network: addressing and routing, as IP does.
Data link: frames on one link, with error checks.
Physical: bits, wavelength, connector and power.

blocks.text: The PDU is a bit at physical, a frame at data link, a packet at network, a segment at transport and a message at application. TCP/IP folds presentation and session into application and uses application, transport, internet and link. Optics touches the physical layer only; a photodiode does not read an IP address.
IP runs over SONET (6.6), over WDM lightpaths, or over Ethernet. Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) puts a short fixed label before each packet; routers switch on the label, not the full IP header.

ATM sends all information in a cell: 53 bytes, a 5-byte header plus a 48-byte payload. The header has a virtual path identifier (VPI) and virtual channel identifier (VCI) to label the connection, a payload type field, a cell loss priority bit and a header error check byte. Short fixed cells suit voice because a sample cannot wait for a long packet. They also let hardware switch fast, with one lookup per cell.

ATM has three layers. Physical moves bits over SONET or fiber. ATM adds and removes the 5-byte header and switches by VPI/VCI. The ATM adaptation layer (AAL) breaks data into cells and rebuilds it. AAL1 carries constant-bit-rate voice and circuit emulation. AAL2 carries compressed voice. AAL5 carries data; it adds an 8-byte trailer, then pads to a multiple of 48 bytes.

Service classes give quality of service (QoS). Constant bit rate (CBR): fixed rate, tight delay, like a call. Real-time variable bit rate (VBR-rt): variable rate, real-time delay. Non-real-time variable bit rate (VBR-nrt): variable rate, no real-time delay. Available bit rate (ABR): feedback shares spare bandwidth. Unspecified bit rate (UBR): no guarantee, like a file download.

ATM lost to IP and Ethernet. IP was already on every computer, Ethernet was cheap and kept getting faster, and ATM paid a cell tax: 5 header bytes per 48 payload bytes. IP over WDM now carries most long-haul traffic. ATM remains in some legacy access and telephone backbones; its QoS classes and label switching ideas survived. Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends labels to wavelengths. The control plane is signalling software that finds a path and sets cross-connects; the data plane is the light.

figure.caption: An IP packet of 1500 bytes drops through the stack: AAL5 adds an 8-byte trailer, padding fills 32 cells of 53 bytes, giving 1696 bytes on the link.

spec.aria: A five-level stack from application to physical, showing that an IP packet of 1500 bytes is carried in 53-byte ATM cells at the data link and as bits at the physical layer.

examples.question: An IP packet of 1500 bytes travels over AAL5, which adds an 8-byte trailer, with a 48-byte cell payload. (a) How many cells are needed? (b) How many bytes go on the link? (c) What is the efficiency?
examples.answer: 32 cells, 1696 bytes on the link, efficiency 88.4 percent.
examples.check:
import math
packet = 1500
trailer = 8
payload = 48
header = 5
total_payload = packet + trailer
cells = math.ceil(total_payload / payload)
link_bytes = cells * (payload + header)
efficiency = packet / link_bytes
print(cells)
print(link_bytes)
print(round(efficiency, 3))

traps: Count the 5-byte header: a 48-byte payload costs 53 bytes, not 48.
Add the AAL5 8-byte trailer and pad before dividing by 48.
Do not confuse VPI with VCI: VPI is the path, VCI is the channel inside it.
AAL1 is constant bit rate voice; AAL5 is data. Swapping them is a common slip.
UBR gives no QoS guarantee; CBR does.

quiz.q: Name the seven OSI layers from top to bottom.
quiz.a: Application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, physical.

quiz.q: Why are ATM cells short and fixed?
quiz.a: Short cells bound voice delay; fixed cells make hardware switching fast and simple.

quiz.q: A 600-byte IP packet uses AAL5 with an 8-byte trailer and 48-byte payload. Find the cells and link bytes.
Why did ATM lose to IP and Ethernet?
quiz.a: IP was already deployed, Ethernet was cheap and faster, and ATM added cell overhead and complexity.

quiz.q: List the five ATM service classes.
Which layer does optics touch, and what is its data unit?
quiz.a: Physical layer; its data unit is a bit.

quiz.q: A voice call needs tight delay but data can wait. Which ATM classes fit each, and why?
quiz.a: Voice: CBR or VBR-rt, because they bound delay. Data: ABR, VBR-nrt or UBR, because they allow variable delay.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, IP over DWDM and MPLS remain the core of metro and backbone networks. ATM still appears in old telephone access and some machine-to-machine links. Researchers now put the control plane on software-defined networking (SDN) controllers. Search for GMPLS, MPLS-TP, segment routing and optical transport network (OTN) switching.
